groups.note: All come from ところ (所, “place”) — placing an event at a certain point in time

items.diff: たところだ ends the sentence and means “just did”; たところで sits mid-sentence and means “even if… (it's no use)”.

this.tr: The train has just left.

that.tr: Even if I run now, I won't make it in time.

items.explain: Look at what follows ところ: if it's 「だ」 and the sentence ends → “just did”; if it's 「で」 and another clause follows, usually a negative or “it's no use” result → “even if…”.

items.diff: たところだ says an action has “just finished”; たところ、 says “I did it, and as a result found…”.

this.tr: I've just sent an email to my teacher.

that.tr: I emailed my teacher, and got a reply right away.

items.explain: At the end of a sentence, 「たところだ」 only marks a point in time; mid-sentence, 「たところ、」 is always followed by a result (often an unexpected discovery), and the whole sentence is in the past tense. If something happens after 「たところ、」, it's the “result” use.

items.diff: ところだ only says what point in time you are at; ところに／へ says “right at that moment, someone or something came along”.

this.tr: I'm just about to go out.

that.tr: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came over.

items.explain: ところに／ところへ is always followed by someone or something that “bursts in” (友達が来た, 電話が鳴った), often disrupting your plans; ところだ only describes your own state, and the sentence ends there.

items.diff: ところだ is a real point in time; ところだった means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: I'm just about to arrive at the station.

that.tr: I very nearly missed the train.

items.explain: Look for words like 「もう少しで」「危うく」 and the past tense 「だった」: ところだった describes something that almost happened but didn't, often with relief or a sense of a close call; ところだ describes a real point in time right now.

groups.note: ところ ↔ どころ — they differ only by the voicing mark (dakuten)

items.diff: ところ means “just now”; どころか means “far from…, in fact / not even…”.

this.tr: I've just finished my homework.

that.tr: Far from finishing my homework, I haven't even started it.

items.explain: First check for the dakuten: ど ≠ と. Then look at the structure: before どころか comes an “expectation”, and after it a fact that is the complete opposite and even more extreme, so the sentence always contrasts two parts.

items.diff: たところだ means “just now”; どころではない means “in no position to… at all”.

this.tr: I've just finished work.

that.tr: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.

items.explain: どころではない usually follows a noun (旅行, 勉強), ends with the negative 「ではない」, and is often preceded by a reason (忙しくて); it has nothing to do with a point in time. If you see ど + a negative at the end, it isn't “just now”.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たところ is objectively “this very moment”; たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”, and can even be used for something months ago.

this.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

that.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → たところ; 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → only たばかり works.

items.diff: たところだ ends the sentence and marks a point in time; たて modifies a noun, stressing “freshly made, brand-new”.

this.tr: The bread has just finished baking.

that.tr: I bought freshly baked bread.

items.explain: たて attaches to a verb's masu-stem (焼き + たて) and is used like an adjective: 「〜たての + noun」. It only works with a handful of verbs (焼きたて, できたて, 生まれたて); to say that something has just happened, use たところだ.

groups.note: Both come from ばかり — originally “only this much”

items.diff: ta-form + ばかり means “just did”; noun + ばかり means “nothing but, all”.

this.tr: I just bought this computer.

that.tr: This shop sells nothing but expensive things.

items.explain: It's the same ばかり, originally meaning “only this”. Look at what comes before it: a ta-form (買った) → “only this little time has passed” = just now; a noun (物) → “only this one kind” = nothing but.

items.diff: たばかり means “just finished doing”; てばかりいる means “always doing, doing nothing but”, often with a complaint.

this.tr: I just ate a little while ago.

that.tr: My little brother does nothing but play games every day.

items.explain: The only difference is た vs. て: た + ばかり is about a short time; て + ばかり + いる is about doing the same thing over and over, and the speaker is often unhappy about it. If you see 「ている」, it means “always”.

groups.note: たばかりだ ↔ たばかりに — they differ only in the last character

items.diff: たばかりだ means “just did”; たばかりに means “just because… (it led to a bad result)”.

this.tr: I've just come to Japan.

that.tr: Just because I said one thing too many, I made her angry.

items.explain: Both are 「た + ばかり」, differing only in the final 「だ」 or 「に」. たばかりに is always followed by a clause with a bad result (〜てしまった), meaning “it was only because of that small thing that…”, often with regret.

groups.note: Both mean “just (now)”

items.diff: たばかり is subjectively “not long ago”; たところだ is objectively “this very moment”.

this.tr: I only came to Japan last month.

that.tr: I've just arrived in Japan (this very moment).

wrong.why: A month has passed, so you can't use たところ

items.explain: Look at the time word: 「先月」 — some time has objectively passed, but the speaker feels it was “not long ago” → たばかり; 「今」 — the action ended right before speaking → both たところ and たばかり work, but たところ puts more stress on “at this very moment”.

items.diff: たばかり works with any verb; たて only attaches to a few verbs and stresses “freshly made, brand-new”.

this.tr: I lost the umbrella I just bought yesterday.

that.tr: Freshly baked bread is delicious.

items.explain: たて attaches directly to the masu-stem (焼き + たて) and is only used with a few words where “the thing made is still new”: 焼きたて, できたて, 生まれたて, 塗りたて. In every other case use たばかり, e.g. 「昨日買ったばかりの傘」.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようになる is a change that happens naturally (“come to…”); ようにする is something you deliberately “make a point of doing”.

this.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

that.tr: I make a point of getting up early for my health.

items.explain: Look at the first half marked with the dotted line: “since my child was born” is an outside cause, and getting up early is the result of changed circumstances → ようになる; “for my health” is your own goal, and getting up early is a habit you consciously keep → ようにする. Memory tip: なる = become, する = do.

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ようになった is a result already achieved; ように is a goal not yet reached that you're still working toward.

this.tr: I practiced every day, so now I can read kanji.

that.tr: I practice every day so that I'll be able to read kanji.

items.explain: Both sentences are about the same thing, just seen from different points in time. Look at what follows ように: if the sentence ends right there → it has already happened (ようになった); if it goes on to say “what you're doing for it” → it's a goal (ように).

items.diff: ようになる means “a person has come to be able to / started to…”; ようになっている means “a machine or system is designed to…”.

this.tr: My child can now get dressed on their own.

that.tr: This door is designed to open automatically when someone approaches.

items.explain: Look at the subject: a person or animal → a change in ability or habit (ようになった); a machine, system or rule → a mechanism designed that way from the start (ようになっている), often together with 「〜と」. It isn't a “change” at all.

groups.note: Both express “change”, but are used differently

items.diff: Both mean “change”; the difference is what they attach to: verbs take ようになる; adjectives and nouns take くなる／になる.

this.tr: I can swim now.

that.tr: I've gotten good at swimming.

wrong.why: A verb can't attach directly to になる

items.explain: First check what kind of word comes before 「なる」: 泳げる is a verb → ようになる; 上手 is a na-adjective → になる (i-adjectives: 寒い → 寒くなる; nouns: 医者 → 医者になる). In English both are just “become / get…”, so learners easily write ✗泳げるになった.

items.diff: ようになる looks at the “end point” of a change (now you can); てくる looks at the “process” (it's changing bit by bit).

this.tr: After three months, I came to understand Japanese.

that.tr: Little by little, I've started to understand Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「３か月で」 sets an end point and describes the new state once it's reached → ようになる; 「少しずつ」 describes the process of change, which is still going on up to now → てくる is common.

groups.note: All come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようにする is something you deliberately “make a point of doing”; ようになる is a change that happens naturally (“come to…”).

this.tr: I make a point of getting up early for my health.

that.tr: Since my child was born, I've (without noticing) started getting up early.

items.explain: Look at the first half marked with the dotted line: “for my health” is your own goal, and getting up early is a habit you consciously keep → ようにする; “since my child was born” is an outside cause, and getting up early is the result of changed circumstances → ようになる. Memory tip: する = do, なる = become.

items.diff: ようにする is your own effort; ように言う is telling someone else to do it.

this.tr: I try to eat vegetables every day.

that.tr: My doctor told me to eat vegetables every day.

items.explain: Look at who made the request: a goal you set for yourself → ようにする; a request from a doctor, teacher or boss → ように言う／ように言われた, often with 「〜に」 before it marking who said it.

groups.note: Both relate to “planning or deciding to do something”

items.diff: ようにする means “try to, make an effort to”, with no guarantee you'll manage every time; ことにする means “decide to”, settled once and for all.

this.tr: I try not to eat sweets.

that.tr: I've decided to give up sweets starting today.

items.explain: Look at the adverbs: 「なるべく」「できるだけ」 often go with ようにする and show the direction of your effort; 「今日から」 with 「ことにした」 shows a decision made at a particular moment.

items.diff: ようにしている is an effort you're already keeping up; つもりだ is a plan in your head that hasn't started yet.

this.tr: I make a point of going to bed by 11 every night.

that.tr: I plan to start going to bed early next week.

items.explain: Look at the time: ようにしている describes a habit you're already doing and keeping up now; つもりだ describes a future plan, and whether it actually happens is still unknown.

groups.note: Both come from the appearance そう — “how something looks”

items.diff: そうだ means “looks like it's going to…”; そうになる means “almost…”, but it didn't actually happen.

this.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

that.tr: I slipped and almost fell.

items.explain: そうだ is a judgment based on what you see in front of you; そうになった is something that “was about to happen to you but in the end didn't”, and is almost always in the past tense 「なった」.

items.diff: そうだ means “looks like it will…”; そうもない means “doesn't look like it will…”.

this.tr: It looks like this work will be finished today.

that.tr: It doesn't look like this work will be finished today.

items.explain: The two sentences differ only in the final 「だ」 vs. 「もない」. The most natural way to negate appearance そうだ is to put the negative after そう: 終わりそうもない／終わりそうにない, meaning “there's no sign at all that it will…”.

groups.note: All mean “seems, looks like”

items.diff: そうだ predicts from how things look (it hasn't happened yet); ようだ infers from evidence (it has most likely already happened).

this.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

that.tr: The road is wet. It seems it has rained.

items.explain: Look at the clue in the first half: you see the state “the sky is dark” and predict what comes next → そうだ (attaches to the masu-stem: 降り + そう); you see the result “the road is wet” and infer what already happened → ようだ (attaches to the plain form: 降った + よう).

items.diff: そうだ (appearance) is what you see with your own eyes; らしい is usually information you heard or got indirectly.

this.tr: This cake looks delicious.

that.tr: According to my friend, the cakes at that shop are supposed to be delicious.

items.explain: Look at the source of the information: the cake is right in front of you → おいしそう; you only heard it from someone and haven't tried it → おいしいらしい. Also note how they attach: そうだ attaches to the stem (おいし + そう), らしい to the plain form (おいしい + らしい).

items.diff: Hearsay そうだ is ordinary reporting; とのことだ is more formal and is often used to pass on someone's message.

this.tr: According to the news, it will snow tomorrow.

that.tr: I have a message from the manager: the meeting starts at 3.

items.explain: Both can mean “I heard that…”, but とのこと is common at work and in letters, with a sense of “I'm passing this on for them”. Also note: hearsay そうだ attaches to the plain form (降る + そうだ); don't confuse it with appearance 降り + そうだ (“looks like it's going to rain”).

groups.note: Both come from よう (様) — “a certain state or way”

items.diff: ようだ is a judgment based on the evidence taken together; ように見える only says how something “looks on the outside”, which may not be true.

this.tr: The lights are off. It seems nobody's home.

that.tr: He looks angry, but he actually isn't.

items.explain: ように見える only describes how something “looks”, and is often followed by 「が、本当は……」, which overturns it; ようだ is the speaker's judgment after putting the clues together, and they basically believe it.

items.diff: ようだ (simile) is an ordinary comparison; かのようだ means “just as if…” about something you know isn't true, so the contrast is stronger.

this.tr: Her hands are as cold as ice.

that.tr: He's smiling as if nothing had happened.

items.explain: かのようだ follows a clause that “isn't actually true” (何もなかった), emphasizing the gap between appearance and reality; ordinary ようだ usually follows “noun + の” and is just a simple comparison.

groups.note: All mean “seems, looks like”

items.diff: ようだ infers from evidence (it has most likely already happened); そうだ predicts from how things look (it hasn't happened yet).

this.tr: The road is wet. It seems it has rained.

that.tr: The sky is dark. It looks like it's going to rain.

items.explain: Look at the clue in the first half: you see the result “the road is wet” and infer what already happened → ようだ (attaches to the plain form: 降った + よう); you see the state “the sky is dark” and predict what comes next → そうだ (attaches to the masu-stem: 降り + そう).

items.diff: ようだ is a judgment based on clues you perceive yourself; らしい is usually based on things you've heard, with a flavor of “reportedly”.

this.tr: I can hear something from the next room. Someone seems to be there.

that.tr: Rumor has it those two are getting married.

items.explain: Look at what the judgment is based on: direct clues you heard or saw yourself → ようだ／みたいだ; indirect information such as rumors or what others said → らしい. With らしい, the speaker sounds detached, as if not taking responsibility for the claim.

groups.note: Both come from はず (筈) — “by reason, logically”

items.diff: はずだ means “logically, it should be so”; はずがない means “logically, it can't possibly be so”.

this.tr: He's lived in Japan for ten years, so he should be able to speak Japanese.

that.tr: He's never studied it even once, so there's no way he can speak Japanese.

items.explain: Look at the reason given in the first half: if it supports the conclusion → はずだ; if it clearly can't lead to the conclusion → はずがない. Note that はずがない is a strong “absolutely impossible”, much stronger than 「話せないはずだ」 (“he shouldn't be able to speak it”).

groups.note: Both mean “judging by logic”

items.diff: はずだ is a logical guess made beforehand; わけだ is “no wonder, so that's why” said afterwards.

this.tr: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive tomorrow.

that.tr: Oh, you sent it yesterday? Then no wonder it's already here.

items.explain: はずだ is for guessing when you don't know the result yet; わけだ is for when you already know the result and, on learning the reason, think “that makes sense”. It's often preceded by 「それなら」「だから」「〜のか」.

items.diff: はずだ has objective grounds (logic); に違いない is a strong subjective conviction (a gut feeling).

this.tr: According to the schedule, the manager should be attending the 3 o'clock meeting.

that.tr: Judging by that smile, something good must have happened.

items.explain: Behind はずだ you can name concrete grounds (a schedule, a rule, a calculation); に違いない is the speaker's own strong feeling, and the grounds can be nothing more than an impression. That's why はずだ is more common when talking about work or in writing.

groups.note: All come from わけ (訳) — “reason, logic”

items.diff: わけだ means “no wonder, naturally”; わけがない means “there's no way”.

this.tr: He practices every day, so no wonder he's good.

that.tr: He's never practiced even once, so there's no way he's good.

items.explain: わけ = reason. わけだ: there's a reason, so “no wonder”; わけがない: there's no such reason at all, so “impossible”. Look at the first half: a solid reason is given → わけだ; the reason obviously doesn't hold → わけがない.

items.diff: わけだ draws the conclusion that logically follows; わけではない means “it's not that…”, a partial denial.

this.tr: Oh, you lived there for three years? No wonder you know Japan so well.

that.tr: I did live in Japan, but that doesn't mean I know it well.

items.explain: わけではない corrects an inference that seems “only natural”: lived in Japan ≠ necessarily knows Japan well. If you see 「けど」 or 「からといって」 earlier in the sentence, what follows is most likely わけではない.

items.diff: わけだ says “that's just how it logically is”; わけにはいかない says “I can't do that, for reasons of logic or responsibility”.

this.tr: Oh, he has an exam tomorrow? So that's why he isn't going out.

that.tr: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and play.

items.explain: The subject of わけにはいかない is usually the speaker, meaning “I'd like to, but because of responsibility, rules or obligations to others, I can't”; わけだ explains a known fact and has nothing to do with whether you “can or can't”.

groups.note: Both mean “judging by logic”

items.diff: わけだ is “no wonder, so that's why” said afterwards; はずだ is a logical guess made beforehand.

this.tr: Oh, you sent it yesterday? Then no wonder it's already here.

that.tr: I sent the package yesterday, so it should arrive tomorrow.

items.explain: わけだ is for when you already know the result and, on learning the reason, think “that makes sense”; it's often preceded by 「それなら」「だから」「〜のか」. はずだ is for guessing when you don't know the result yet.

groups.note: Both come from ため (為) — “purpose, cause”

items.diff: ために sits inside the sentence, right after the cause or purpose; そのため starts a sentence and refers back to the previous one.

this.tr: The trains stopped because of heavy snow.

that.tr: There was heavy snow last night. Because of that, the trains stopped.

items.explain: Same meaning, different position: ために comes right after the cause, all in one sentence; そのため is a standalone conjunction that needs a sentence before it, and 「その」 refers to what that sentence said.

groups.note: All mean “in order to” or “because”

items.title: 〜ように (purpose)
items.diff: ために follows actions you can control; ように follows states, such as potential or negative forms.

this.tr: I study every day in order to pass the N1.

that.tr: I study every day so that I can speak Japanese.

wrong.why: After a potential form, use ように

items.explain: Look at the verb before ため／ように: 「合格する」 is an action you decide to do → ために; potential forms, negative forms and things that happen on their own, like 「話せる」「忘れない」「見える」 → ように.

items.title: 〜から (reason)
items.diff: ために (cause) is more formal/written and is followed by an objective result that has already happened; から is more conversational and can be followed by invitations, requests or commands.

this.tr: The trains are delayed due to an accident.

that.tr: We're out of time, so let's hurry.

wrong.why: ために of cause can't be followed by an invitation or command

items.explain: Look at the second half: stating a result that has already happened, like a station announcement or the news → ために; your own invitation or request, like 「〜よう」「〜てください」 → only から (or ので) works.

items.title: 〜には (purpose)
items.diff: ために is followed by “what you do”; には is followed by “what's needed, what it takes”.

this.tr: I'm saving money to buy a house.

that.tr: To buy a house, you need a lot of money.

items.explain: Look at the second half: an action you're taking (貯金している) → ために; a need or evaluation such as 「必要だ」「〜がかかる」「〜がいい」 → には.

groups.note: All come from こと (事) — turning an action into the content of a decision

items.diff: ことにする is your own decision; ことになる is decided by others or by circumstances.

this.tr: After thinking it over myself, I decided to quit my job.

that.tr: On the company's orders, I'm being transferred to Osaka.

items.explain: Look at who made the decision: 「自分で考えて」 → ことにした; 「会社の命令で」 → ことになった. Also, Japanese speakers sometimes deliberately use ことになった for their own decisions, to sound modest and low-key.

items.diff: ことにした is a decision made at one moment; ことにしている is a personal rule kept up over a long time.

this.tr: Starting today, I've decided to go running every morning.

that.tr: For five years now, I've made a point of running every morning.

items.explain: Look at the time words: 「今日から」 marks the moment of deciding → ことにした; 「もう５年」「いつも」 show it's been kept up for a long time → ことにしている.

items.diff: ことにする is a personal decision; ことになっている is a rule, a system, or an arrangement settled in advance.

this.tr: I've decided not to look at my phone at night.

that.tr: In this dorm, you're not allowed to go out after 10 p.m.

items.explain: Look at where the decision comes from: something you set for yourself → ことにする／ことにした; the rules of a school, company or dorm, or an arrangement agreed on in advance → ことになっている.

groups.note: Both relate to “planning or deciding to do something”

items.diff: ことにした is the moment you make up your mind; つもりだ is a plan you've had in mind.

this.tr: I hesitated for a long time, but I've decided to study abroad.

that.tr: I plan to study abroad next year.

items.explain: ことにした often carries a sense of “finally deciding after hesitating” (迷ったけど, いろいろ考えて); つもりだ just states an intention without stressing the moment of decision, and you might not end up going.

items.diff: ことにする follows a verb; にする follows a noun and is often used to pick one of several options.

this.tr: I've decided to go to Okinawa for summer vacation.

that.tr: For my drink, I'll have coffee.

wrong.why: After a verb, you need 「こと」

items.explain: First check whether a verb or a noun comes before it: 行く (verb) → ことにする; コーヒー (noun) → にする. 「〜にします」 is most common when ordering food or choosing something.
